e2v.title: Evolution favours organisms that feel their own temperature. A volatile climate doesn't make that stronger.
e2v.verdict_label: Pre-registered hypothesis not supported · ρ = +0.01, p = 0.46
e2v.summary: The prediction was that self-sensing pays off more as the climate gets more volatile, the way estuary animals regulate their salt balance and open-ocean ones don't. That prediction failed. What the competition showed instead is that self-sensing wins almost everywhere, including a perfectly constant climate. This reverses an earlier analysis from July 2026, which compared populations in separate worlds and switched off sensing by zeroing inputs. Under a fair control, the earlier result flips.
stats: worlds where self-sensing organisms took over the population (binomial p = 4×10⁻¹¹)
longer lifespan for self-sensing organisms: 82 vs 66 steps, p = 5×10⁻⁷ (exploratory)
yoking only the temperature reading reproduces the whole advantage; energy and damage don't (exploratory)
e2v.scope: What this does not show: that the organisms are regulating their temperature in the physiological sense. Their body temperature tracks the weather exactly as much as the yoked organisms' does, and probing their controllers shows no 'slow down when hot' reflex. Selection clearly uses self-temperature information, but we have not yet found how. That is the next experiment.

hab1.title: On a simpler body, the self-regulating agent trended better, but not reliably enough to pass.
hab1.verdict_label: Pre-registered test failed · best damage type p = 0.08 (0.23 after correction)
hab1.summary: MuJoCo's Ant, a four-legged body where running fast generates heat that damages it. The self-regulating agent survived about 40% longer under sensor noise and metabolic stress and was ahead at 16 of 20 damage levels. With 6 training seeds, though, the difference isn't statistically reliable. The physics also turned out harsher than intended: even with no damage, the standard agent overheated and died before the end in 98% of episodes, so the baseline was already a damaged condition.
stats: damage levels where the self-regulating agent survived longer (sign test p = 0.012, secondary)
survival under sensor and metabolic damage (effect size g ≈ 1.0), not significant with 6 seeds
undamaged episodes finished by the standard vs self-regulating agent; most deaths were heat damage
hab1.scope: What this does not show: graceful degradation. Under sensor and metabolic damage the gap is the same as with no damage at all, and moderate leg damage actually helped both agents by slowing them down and cooling them. A conclusive replication needs about 16 to 21 seeds per condition and physics that leave a healthy undamaged baseline. That lesson shaped the Go2 experiment.

go2.title: Does a robot that manages its own motor heat get further on a long, loaded mission?
go2.verdict_label: Pre-registered test failed, and this time it was a valid test · loaded missions p = 0.64
go2.summary: Second version, fixing everything that made the first one uninformative. The missions last 3 minutes with up to 6 kg on the robot's back, long enough for motors to overheat. A gate confirms the self-regulating robot really runs cooler (it did: 0.75 vs 0.83). Against standard robots, a hand-written thermal governor of the kind used in industry, and a version with a learned model of its own body in the loop, the self-regulating robot did not get further on loaded missions. What happened instead is the useful part: unloaded it walks just as far with cooler motors, but under load it sometimes freezes instead of pacing itself, and it ignores its own self-model.
stats: unloaded: the same 156 m walked in 3 minutes with the hottest motor running cooler (exploratory)
loaded missions in which the self-regulating robot froze instead of pacing itself (exploratory)
cutting the self-model out of the loop changed nothing: the robot learned a model of itself but didn't use it
go2.scope: What this shows: making a robot averse to heat is not the same as making it manage heat well. Pacing a 3-minute mission is a long-horizon skill, and these policies were trained on 20-second episodes. A self-model only matters if decisions go through it. The next version trains on full missions and charges the robot for predicted overheating, not just current temperature.
go2.figure_caption: HAB-P2: (a) pre-registered metric, net distance in a 3-minute mission (huge spread, because every controller drifts off heading); (b) hottest-motor temperature, where the treatment gate passed unloaded; (c) the same self-model robots with the loop intact vs cut: no difference.

Here the self-regulating robot walks 14.6 m and the standard one 1.6 m, but both run their motors equally hot, and across all trained robots the difference is not reliable.
